lesson_title: The Pull That Never Lets Go: Universal Gravitation
hook_text: You are pulling on the Moon right now. The Moon is pulling back. Same formula, same force, both directions.
clip_script: Right now, you are pulling on your desk, on the learner next to you, on Table Mountain, on the Moon. Everything with mass pulls on everything else — that is what universal means. So why don't you feel your desk tugging you sideways? Because gravity is pathetic unless one partner is a planet. Two learners a metre apart attract each other with a third of a MILLIONTH of a newton. Swap one learner for the Earth and its ten-to-the-24 kilograms, and suddenly the pull is 686 newtons — your weight. The rules are simple. More mass, more pull. More distance, much less pull: double the gap and the force drops to a QUARTER, because distance always gets squared. And here's the twist nobody believes — the Earth pulls you with 686 newtons, and you pull the Earth up with exactly 686 newtons. The Earth just doesn't care, because 686 newtons on ten-to-the-24 kilograms moves it less than an atom's width. Go to the Moon and your mass stays the same, but each kilogram gets only 1,62 newtons of pull instead of 9,8. Same you. Different weight.
visual_style: Faint glowing threads connecting a learner to desk, classmates, mountain and Moon; the Earth thread thickening dramatically; a distance slider quartering a force meter; a scale reading dropping as the scene shifts from Earth to Moon.
mood: Quietly mind-blowing — the invisible made visible in an ordinary classroom.
pacing: Slow wonder to open, brisk rule-by-rule middle, gentle drop on the final line.
